About Shakespeare

William Shakespeare, who lived over four hundred years ago in England, is the most famous writer in the English language. He wrote around thirty-seven plays, comedies, histories and tragedies, that are still performed all over the world today. A tragedy is a play that ends in sorrow, and often teaches a hard truth: The Tempest shows the power of forgiveness, Macbeth the ruin of greedy ambition, and Romeo and Juliet the terrible cost of hatred. These retellings share the stories in simple form; the plays themselves are written in beautiful poetry well worth discovering when you are older.

You may already know the tale of The Tempest, of Prospero the magician wronged by his brother and cast out to sea with his young daughter Miranda. On a lonely enchanted island, Prospero raised his daughter and grew mighty in magic, served by an airy spirit named Ariel.

image.note: The magician Prospero on an enchanted island shore, his daughter Miranda beside him, a shimmering spirit in the air

pages.text: When the very brother who had betrayed him sailed near the island, Prospero raised a great storm, a tempest, to wreck the ship and bring his enemies ashore, unharmed but scattered and afraid. He had them all in his power at last, and could have taken any revenge he wished upon the men who had ruined him.

image.note: A ship tossed in a magical storm near the island; frightened men washing ashore unhurt; the magician watching

pages.text: Meanwhile, Miranda met a kind young prince from the wrecked ship, and the two fell gently in love, which quietly pleased her father. But the great question of the tale was this: now that Prospero held his enemies helpless, would he choose cruel revenge, or would he choose to forgive?

image.note: Miranda and a young prince meeting shyly on the shore, drawn to each other; Prospero observing, thoughtful

pages.text: And here Prospero showed true greatness. Though he had every reason for revenge, he chose instead to forgive his brother and make peace. He set his faithful spirit Ariel free, gave up his magic forever, and prepared to sail home with his daughter and her prince. Mercy, the story teaches, is a nobler thing than revenge.

image.note: Prospero forgiving his kneeling brother, breaking his magic staff; Ariel flying free; mercy over vengeance; warm

pages.text: The Tempest is a tale of storms and magic, but its heart is gentle: that it is braver to forgive an enemy than to punish him, and wiser to let go of anger than to hold it. Now we turn to a darker tale, of a man who chose the very opposite path, and paid a terrible price for it.

image.note: The island fading behind a departing ship, Prospero and Miranda aboard; a peaceful close to the first tale

pages.text: In wild and misty Scotland long ago, there lived a brave and honoured soldier named Macbeth. Returning from a great victory, he and his friend Banquo met three strange witches upon a lonely heath. The witches spoke a prophecy that would poison Macbeth's heart. They hailed him, and foretold that he would one day be king.

image.note: Three eerie witches on a misty Scottish heath confronting two soldiers; a fateful prophecy; ominous

pages.text: The words lit a dangerous fire of ambition in Macbeth. He wrote of the prophecy to his wife, Lady Macbeth, and she was even more ambitious than he. When the good old king came to stay as a guest in their castle, she urged her husband to a terrible deed: to murder the king in his sleep and seize the crown at once.

image.note: Lady Macbeth urging her troubled husband on by candlelight; a crown gleaming in his mind; temptation, darkness

pages.text: Torn and terrified, Macbeth let ambition overrule his conscience. That night he crept into the king's chamber and did the dreadful deed, and by morning he was king. But he had bought the crown with a crime, and from that moment neither he nor his wife knew a single hour of peace again. Guilt began to eat them both alive.

image.note: Macbeth standing shaken outside a chamber, a look of horror on his face; the deed done offstage; guilt, not gore

pages.text: One murder led to another. To keep his stolen crown safe, Macbeth killed again and again, growing crueller and more feared, until the whole land groaned under his tyranny. Lady Macbeth, tormented by guilt, walked in her sleep, endlessly trying to wash imagined blood from her hands, and at last her troubled mind gave way entirely.

image.note: Lady Macbeth sleepwalking, wringing her hands as if washing them; haunted and broken; the cost of the crime

pages.text: In the end, the murdered king's son raised an army and marched against the tyrant. Macbeth, who had trusted the witches to the last, found their promises had tricked him, and he fell in battle. So ended the man who had thrown away his honour for a crown. Ambition without conscience, the tale warns, destroys the one who follows it.

image.note: An army marching on a dark castle; Macbeth facing his doom; the tyrant fallen, the rightful heir restored; solemn

pages.text: In the fair city of Verona lived two great families, the Montagues and the Capulets, who hated one another with an ancient and bitter feud. Their quarrels spilled into the streets, and no one could remember how the hatred had even begun. Into this world of feuding were born two young people who would change everything.

image.note: Two noble families brawling in an Italian street; an ancient feud; a divided city; tension

pages.text: Romeo, a young Montague, slipped into a grand feast at the Capulet house, and there he saw Juliet, a young Capulet, and the two fell instantly and deeply in love, not knowing at first that their families were sworn enemies. When they learned the truth, it was already too late. Their hearts were given, whatever their families might say.

image.note: Romeo and Juliet meeting at a masked feast, love at first sight; the balcony scene; tender, star-crossed

pages.text: Knowing their families would never allow it, the two were secretly married by a kindly friar, who hoped their love might one day heal the feud. But fate was cruel. A street fight broke out between the families, lives were lost on both sides, and Romeo was banished from the city, torn from his new bride almost as soon as he had wed her.

image.note: A secret wedding by a gentle friar; then a tragic street fight; Romeo banished, the lovers parted; sorrowful

pages.text: The friar made a desperate plan to reunite them, but a message went astray, and everything went tragically wrong. Through a chain of misunderstandings, both young lovers came to grief, each believing the other lost. Their deaths were not wicked, like Macbeth's, but a terrible accident born of hatred and haste, and they are mourned to this day.

image.note: The two young lovers parted forever by tragic mistake; the gentle friar grieving; loss, not violence; tender sorrow

pages.text: When the two families saw what their hatred had cost them, their grief broke the ancient feud at last. Standing together over their lost children, the Montagues and Capulets finally made peace, though at the bitterest possible price. The great tragedy teaches that hatred handed down through generations harms, in the end, the very ones we love most.

image.note: The two grieving families reconciling at last, clasping hands in sorrow; peace bought too dearly; a solemn close
